Chapter 4. Critique of Utilitarianism and the Priority of Rights
Finding the right balance between individual rights and the common good is one of the biggest challenges any theory of justice has to tackle.
Utilitarianism, for example, says the best society is the one that creates the most happiness for the most people. That sounds reasonable at first, doesn’t it?
But there’s a problem: sometimes, this approach means the interests of a few get sacrificed for the sake of everyone else.
Now, let’s look at a different way of thinking—justice as fairness. This idea insists that our basic rights and liberties aren’t up for negotiation, even if giving them up would make more people happy overall.
This is what’s called the priority of rights. In other words, those fundamental freedoms outlined in the first principle of justice have to be protected, no matter how tempting it might be to limit them for some greater good.
This critique of utilitarianism really comes down to one thing: treating every person as an end in themselves—not just as a tool to make someone else happier.
Think about it. In a utilitarian world, it’s possible for the rights of a minority to get pushed aside if it means the majority ends up happier.
But justice as fairness says, “Wait a minute. The rights and interests of every single person matter. We can’t just ignore them.”
There’s another idea that helps set justice as fairness apart—the difference principle. Rather than focusing on simply making society richer or happier overall, it asks a different question: do social and economic inequalities actually help the people who have the least?
This shift means we’re always keeping the well-being of the most vulnerable front and center.
To see why utilitarianism can fall short, let’s imagine a situation: a small group is forced to carry heavy burdens so that the majority gets bigger benefits.
Sure, the overall happiness might go up—but for those who are disadvantaged, it’s deeply unfair.
Justice as fairness avoids this by demanding that any inequality has to be justified in terms of how it affects the least advantaged among us.
So, when you put the priority of rights and the difference principle together, you end up with a system that respects each person’s dignity and still promotes equality across society.
It’s a solid alternative to utilitarianism—one that makes sure justice isn’t just about adding up happiness, but about truly protecting the rights and interests of everyone.
